senses.gloss:
1. Koka, a word occurring in the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda, seems to denote the ‘cuckoo.’ In all the three passages in which it is found, Sāyaṇa explains it as the cakravāka. Roth renders it in the Atharvaveda passages as a certain destructive parasitic animal. Cf. anyavāpa.
Foot notes vii. 104, 22 (koka-yātu, a ghost in the shape of a cuckoo).
v. 23, 4; viii. 6, 2.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v., 6.
Cf. Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 454; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 262; Geldner, Rigveda, Glossar, 49; Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 92.
2. Koka is mentioned in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 17) as a son of the pañcāla king, sātrāsāha.

Kokila, a very frequent word in the Epic and later, denoting the cuckoo, is only inferred for the Vedic period from its being the name of a rājaputra in the kāṭhaka Anukramaṇī.
Foot notes Weber, Indische Studien, 3, 460.
